commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>

[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

commit_message:
[Python] Add Torch dialect registration modules (#25251)

I hit this while profiling PyTorch graph import through Turbine/IREE.
MLIR's Python bindings look for `iree.compiler.dialects.torch` and
`torch_c`, but neither module exists. Failed dialect imports are retried
during type construction and operation inspection, producing roughly
38,000 failed lookups for D-FINE.

This adds standard Python namespace registrations for the existing
native Torch and TorchConversion dialects and includes them in the
Python package. Operations continue to use generic OpViews.

I've added coverage to the existing registration test, which fails
before and passes after the change. With LLVM/MLIR 23.1.2 in Wasm64,
D-FINE's graph import/preparation dropped from 15.3 s to 1.9 s, and its
first model call from 45.8 s to 32.0 s. CPU and WebGPU correctness
checks still pass.

Signed-off-by: anutosh491 <andersonbhat491@gmail.com>
name: setup_metadata

commit_message:
Integrate LLVM to llvm/llvm-project@143db483b8b9

The following fix needs to be kept:
 - [mlir][VectorToGPU] Reconsider cached slices after rejected
   candidates

We also needed to fold slices of empty tensors before scf.forall
canonicalization would tie them to `shared_outs`, due to changes
introduced in:

commit_message:
Integrate LLVM to llvm/llvm-project@143db483b8b9

The following fix needs to be kept:
 - [mlir][VectorToGPU] Reconsider cached slices after rejected
   candidates

We also needed to fold slices of empty tensors before scf.forall
canonicalization would tie them to `shared_outs`, due to changes
introduced in:
 - https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/241838

A GPU lit test had to be adjusted to account for that as well.

The TOSA allowNonFinities option had to be explicitly set back to false,
to not break WebGPU. The default was changed in upstream MLIR:
 - https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/239407

The bump also exposed pre-existing UB, fixed by replacing std::abs
with llvm::AbsoluteValue.

commit_message:
Integrate LLVM to llvm/llvm-project@143db483b8b9

The following fix needs to be kept:
 - [mlir][VectorToGPU] Reconsider cached slices after rejected
   candidates

We also needed to fold slices of empty tensors before scf.forall
canonicalization would tie them to `shared_outs`, due to changes
introduced in:
 - https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/241838

A GPU lit test had to be adjusted to account for that as well.

The TOSA allowNonFinities option had to be explicitly set back to false,
to not break WebGPU. The default was changed in upstream MLIR:
 - https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/239407

The bump also exposed pre-existing UB, fixed by replacing std::abs
with llvm::AbsoluteValue.

commit_message:
[HIP] Keep allocation completion ordered with its signal stream (#25291)

Queue allocations run on the async memory stream and record their
signal-semaphore events there. The cleanup event that advances those
semaphores on the host, however, was always recorded on the dispatch
stream. Allocation completion was therefore observed independently of
the stream that performed it.

`iree_hal_hip_device_stream_add_cleanup` now records on the stream it is
given, and semaphore signalling passes the stream its events were
recorded on. Queue reads and submissions keep using the dispatch stream.

Assisted-by: Codex

Queue allocations run on the async memory stream and record their
signal-semaphore events there. The cleanup event that advances those
semaphores on the host, however, was always recorded on the dispatch
stream. Allocation completion was therefore observed independently of
the stream that performed it.

`iree_hal_hip_device_stream_add_cleanup` now records on the stream it is
given, and semaphore signalling passes the stream its events were
recorded on. Queue reads and submissions keep using the dispatch stream.

Assisted-by: Codex

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Add an option to limit the bytes a dispatch binds

Some targets need to have every buffer a dispatch binds mapped to a limited
address space, e.g. 32 bit. There may also be other limits on the amount of
mapped memory at the same time. Fusion can form dispatches that cannot run,
even when each binding fits into the max allocation size. For instance,
once a large constant is split into shards (see
`iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`), elementwise fusion merges the
per-shard embedding lookups back into one op that reads every shard.

This adds `--iree-dispatch-creation-max-dispatch-binding-bytes` (default 0,
no limit) and a `max-binding-bytes` option on the passes that grow
dispatches:

* ElementwiseOpFusion, for fusion outside of dispatches,
* FuseMultiUseElementwiseProducer, for fusion outside of dispatches,
* FormDispatchRegions, in `FusionGroup::wouldExceedOperandLimit`, next to
  the existing limit on the number of operands, so that all producer and
  consumer fusion decisions are covered,
* CloneProducersIntoDispatchRegions, through `CloneableIntoDispatchOptions`
  in `getCloneableOps`,
* FuseHorizontalContractions, which adds a weight and a result to the
  fused contraction for each contraction it merges,
* ConvertTensorToFlow, for producers cloned into the dispatches it
  creates for slices.

The bytes are estimated by `IREE::Flow::getDispatchBindingBytes`: the
statically shaped tensors that the ops read from outside (as operands or
captured in their regions), plus their results that are used outside. Loads
of the same global count once; `tensor.empty`, `linalg.fill` and splat
constants are not bindings. Producers cloned into a dispatch contribute only
what they read, because those remain in place for their other users.
Fusion decisions count the producers that CloneProducersIntoDispatchRegions
will clone into the dispatch later (e.g. dequantization ops) by what they
read, not by their results. A fusion or clone is refused only if the dispatch
would then bind more than the limit and more than it did without it, so fusions
that shrink a dispatch already over the limit still happen.

Dynamically shaped tensors count as zero bytes, so the limit only covers
static shapes, which includes all constants.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>
name: setup / setup

address space, e.g. 32 bit. There may also be other limits on the amount of
mapped memory at the same time. Fusion can form dispatches that cannot run,
even when each binding fits into the max allocation size. For instance,
once a large constant is split into shards (see
`iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`), elementwise fusion merges the
per-shard embedding lookups back into one op that reads every shard.

This adds `--iree-dispatch-creation-max-dispatch-binding-bytes` (default 0,
no limit) and a `max-binding-bytes` option on the passes that grow
dispatches:

* ElementwiseOpFusion, for fusion outside of dispatches,
* FuseMultiUseElementwiseProducer, for fusion outside of dispatches,
* FormDispatchRegions, in `FusionGroup::wouldExceedOperandLimit`, next to
  the existing limit on the number of operands, so that all producer and
  consumer fusion decisions are covered,
* CloneProducersIntoDispatchRegions, through `CloneableIntoDispatchOptions`
  in `getCloneableOps`,
* FuseHorizontalContractions, which adds a weight and a result to the
  fused contraction for each contraction it merges,
* ConvertTensorToFlow, for producers cloned into the dispatches it
  creates for slices.

The bytes are estimated by `IREE::Flow::getDispatchBindingBytes`: the
statically shaped tensors that the ops read from outside (as operands or
captured in their regions), plus their results that are used outside. Loads
of the same global count once; `tensor.empty`, `linalg.fill` and splat
constants are not bindings. Producers cloned into a dispatch contribute only
what they read, because those remain in place for their other users.
Fusion decisions count the producers that CloneProducersIntoDispatchRegions
will clone into the dispatch later (e.g. dequantization ops) by what they
read, not by their results. A fusion or clone is refused only if the dispatch
would then bind more than the limit and more than it did without it, so fusions
that shrink a dispatch already over the limit still happen.

Dynamically shaped tensors count as zero bytes, so the limit only covers
static shapes, which includes all constants.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Honor --iree-llvmcpu-skip-intermediate-roundings=false for RVV Zvfhmin f16 inner_tiled MMA

Zvfhmin lacks native f16 MAC, so f16 MMA widens accumulator to f32
then truncates back. These extf/truncf pairs were marked as invertible
and hoisted out of K loop, dropping per-K rounding and producing wrong
answers. The skip-intermediate-roundings flag was not plumbed into
lowering at all.

Propagate skipIntermediateRoundings through inner tile lowering and the
LLVMCPU vector pipelines. When we need to preserve roundings (widenF16Acc
&& !skipIntermediateRoundings), materialize the f16 -> f32 -> f16
round-trip directly around each MA step in emitIntrinsic, and drop the
hoistable distribute/reassemble accumulator pair.

Add tests covering both keep-rounding and skip-rounding modes.

Fixes: iree-org/iree#25058
Assisted-by: Claude Code, Doubao, DeepSeek
Signed-off-by: Yalong <yalong@multicorewareinc.com>
name: setup / setup

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Honor --iree-llvmcpu-skip-intermediate-roundings=false for RVV Zvfhmin f16 inner_tiled MMA

Zvfhmin lacks native f16 MAC, so f16 MMA widens accumulator to f32
then truncates back. These extf/truncf pairs were marked as invertible
and hoisted out of K loop, dropping per-K rounding and producing wrong
answers. The skip-intermediate-roundings flag was not plumbed into
lowering at all.

Propagate skipIntermediateRoundings through inner tile lowering and the
LLVMCPU vector pipelines. When we need to preserve roundings (widenF16Acc
&& !skipIntermediateRoundings), materialize the f16 -> f32 -> f16
round-trip directly around each MA step in emitIntrinsic, and drop the
hoistable distribute/reassemble accumulator pair.

Add tests covering both keep-rounding and skip-rounding modes.

commit_message:
[Python] Add Torch dialect registration modules (#25251)

I hit this while profiling PyTorch graph import through Turbine/IREE.
MLIR's Python bindings look for `iree.compiler.dialects.torch` and
`torch_c`, but neither module exists. Failed dialect imports are retried
during type construction and operation inspection, producing roughly
38,000 failed lookups for D-FINE.

This adds standard Python namespace registrations for the existing
native Torch and TorchConversion dialects and includes them in the
Python package. Operations continue to use generic OpViews.

I've added coverage to the existing registration test, which fails
before and passes after the change. With LLVM/MLIR 23.1.2 in Wasm64,
D-FINE's graph import/preparation dropped from 15.3 s to 1.9 s, and its
first model call from 45.8 s to 32.0 s. CPU and WebGPU correctness
checks still pass.

Signed-off-by: anutosh491 <andersonbhat491@gmail.com>
name: linux-aarch64 :: Build main-dist-linux Package

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schuermans <schuermans@roofline.ai>
name: runtime_tracing :: windows-2022 :: tracy

config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
expressions are hoisted and evaluated into new globals.

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Split constants larger than the max allocation size

A constant whose storage exceeds the max allocation size of its resource
config cannot be packed within that limit. PackConstants places such
constants in a separate resource, but the size will still exceed the limit.
The problem only shows up at runtime, when the device fails to allocate
the buffer.

This adds `iree-global-opt-split-large-constants`. It splits a private,
immutable global above the limit into shards along its outermost non-unit
dimension. Each resulting shard is a contiguous byte range of the original
constant and fits into one allocation. The initial value can be an inline
dense constant, which is sliced, or a named parameter, which is not read: each
shard refers to its byte range of the same parameter through the `offset` and
`length` config entries, relative to any offset the parameter already has. The
uses of its loads are rewritten to use the shards:

* An input of a structured op whose split dimension is indexed by a single
  loop: the op is split along that loop with TilingInterface, one op per
  shard. The results of a parallel loop are inserted into the destination.
  The ops of a reduction loop accumulate into the previous result. This
  covers matmuls with a large weight, such as a tied LM head.
* A value read with `tensor.extract` in the body of an elementwise
  `linalg.generic`, e.g., an embedding lookup: a chain of ops, one per
  shard. Each reads its shard at the rebased, clamped index and keeps the
  previous op's element unless the index lies in its shard.

A constant with any other use is left unchanged with a warning, as is one
that cannot be split: mutable or public globals, values that are neither
inline dense constants nor named parameters, parameters whose length does not
match their type or whose offset is not an integer, element types not stored
at 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits, or a single index of the split dimension that alone
exceeds the limit.

The limit is the max allocation size from `ResourceConfigAttr::lookup`, so
`--iree-stream-resource-max-allocation-size` unless the target sets one. It
defaults to INT64_MAX, so the pass changes nothing unless a limit is set. The
pass runs after transposes have been folded into their consumers, so that an
oversized constant is read by the op that indexes it, and before constant
